item.title: Two-sample Behrens-Fisher problems for high-dimensional data: noncentral normal-reference inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.14598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study noncentral normal-reference inference for high-dimensional two-sample Behrens-Fisher problems. Within the Gaussian reference, a shifted null law is accurate if and only if covariance-weighted signal energy is negligible relative to the trace of the squared covariance. We establish the sharp uniform fourth-root error order over unrestricted spectra and a linear bound under spectral spread. A separate spectral-range criterion determines when signal magnitude alone suffices. An augmented spherical reference gives finite-sample calibration for Gaussian samples and asymptotically recovers Gaussian-reference local power under projection fourth-moment bounds and control of diagonal fluctuations, without a dimension-to-sample-size restriction. For unknown Gaussian covariance, explicit trace and hollow-Gram confidence bounds turn the linear approximation bound into a simultaneous, computable certificate over local effect ranges. Eigenspace signal energies describe directional power, while a two-point argument limits estimation of unknown local power. Simulations with 10,000 evaluation replications per configuration examine unequal and noncommuting covariances, severe sample imbalance, non-Gaussian observations and the informativeness of the certificate.
item.dc:creator: Pengfei Wang

item.title: The exact region of the Average Rectangular Volume and Spearman's rho, with an application to arachnitude
item.description: arXiv:2611.14645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The average rectangular volume ($\ARV$) of a bivariate aggregation function is the average of its volumes over all axis-parallel rectangles of the unit square; for a copula, it is the expected copula volume of the rectangle spanned by two independent uniform points. We determine the exact region of the pairs $(\ARV(C),\rho(C))$, where $C$ ranges over all bivariate copulas and $\rho$ is Spearman's rho. The region is compact, convex and symmetric, and its upper boundary consists of three analytically parametrized arcs. A previously proposed family of shuffles of Min generates one arc, but only on part of its range; the other two arcs are generated by singular copulas whose supports contain hyperbolic branches. The boundary is continuously differentiable away from its left endpoint $\ARV=\frac{11}{120}$, where it has a vertical tangent. The proof uses a folding transformation and explicit Kantorovich potentials for a family of optimal transport problems. Finally, we show that the arachnitude, a rank correlation used in actuarial practice, is an affine transformation of $\ARV$, so that the result also describes the joint region of Spearman's rho and arachnitude.
item.dc:creator: Luca Anzilli, Fabrizio Durante

item.title: Fundamental Limits of Honest Inference with Heterogeneous Transfer Sources
item.description: arXiv:2611.14684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transfer learning can improve precision by borrowing information from external sources, but how much improvement is possible while maintaining valid inference? We address this by studying honest confidence intervals for a target parameter using multiple sources with heterogeneous prespecified discrepancy bounds. Under local information and admissibility conditions, we establish a universal lower bound on interval length for procedures maintaining uniform coverage. A scalar information equation characterizes the bound, revealing how precision depends jointly on source sample sizes and discrepancies. Large source samples need not yield greater precision gains when their discrepancies are large. When discrepancies are unrestricted, honest intervals cannot improve upon the target-only rate, even when all sources are unbiased. For the Gaussian location model, we calculate optimal source weights and construct honest intervals attaining the lower bound order, establishing sharpness. We extend the lower bound theory to semiparametric models through parametric submodels. For the Cox proportional hazards model, we verify the information conditions under which the lower bound applies, including under right censoring.
item.dc:creator: Xuran Meng, Yi Li

item.title: Discrete total variation under the multinomial, Part 5: cyclic total variation
item.description: arXiv:2611.14735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the cyclic discrete total variation obtained by adding the wrap-around edge to the usual open-chain statistic. Under the uniform multinomial law the cyclic symmetry recombines the same per-edge, adjacent, and disjoint covariance blocks used for the linear statistic, but with different multiplicities, and this simplifies the variance: the bin-independent leading coefficient \(2A+4B\) carries over, the constant-order correction collapses \emph{exactly} to \(\beta_c(n)=\beta_1 n\) (no \(n^0\) or \(1/n\) tail; obtained directly here, and already reached in Part~2 through the transfer identity), and a conditional second-order coefficient \(\gamma_c(n)\) is given. The exact finite-\(N\) cyclic--linear transfer identity of Part~2, read order by order, both delivers these and, as its main consequence for the \emph{linear} statistic, explains the traveling mode of the linear variance: comparison with the (first-order) mode-free symmetric cyclic profile shows that deleting one edge introduces a rising contribution whose balance against the falling cyclic bulk creates a ridge at \(n\asymp\sqrt{K_0N}\) with local optimizer \(K_0=C_1/\beta_1\). Uniform control of three ridge blocks proves this optimizer on every compact ridge window, upgrading the previously heuristic \(\sqrt N\) mode law to a theorem; the global localization of the exact maximizer remains open. We also record the corresponding cyclic reference-centered statistic under a fixed alternative and the leading Nabeya variance formula for the matched non-uniform cyclic statistic. Throughout, ``exact'' refers to the asymptotic coefficient in \(N\); the operative symmetry is cyclic stationarity (rotation invariance), not exchangeability.
item.dc:creator: Nikola Bani\'c, Neven Elezovi\'c

item.title: Asymptotic Consistency of a Weighted Nadaraya-Watson Estimator Driven by Fractional Brownian Motion at Random Times
item.description: arXiv:2611.14737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonparametric regression conventionally assumes equispaced observations, a premise often violated by empirical data with irregular sampling and long-memory noise. This study establishes the asymptotic mean square ($L^2$) consistency of a weighted Nadaraya-Watson (wN-W) estimator for stochastic processes sampled at random times and perturbed by fractional Brownian motion (fBm). Leveraging the occupation time formula and Fernique's Theorem, we derive exact parametric restrictions on bandwidth and sampling rates ensuring convergence. We validate these theoretical findings via extensive simulations evaluating the mean squared error under varying noise persistence. Crucially, we explicitly benchmark the performance of the estimator under random sampling times against classical deterministic grids, while assessing the relative efficiency of quartic versus Gaussian kernels. Finally, we introduce an interactive Shiny application to dynamically visualize the admissible parameter space, and we empirically validate our theoretical framework by applying the estimator to the Vostok ice core paleoclimatological dataset. This real-world application demonstrates the practical capacity of the methodology to extract macroscopic trends while robustly avoiding severe overfitting under random sampling times.\
item.dc:creator: Tania Roa, Meryem Slaoui, Soledad Torres

item.title: Beyond weak convergence of signed spectral measures: Eigenvector overlaps and high-dimensional prediction risk
item.description: arXiv:2611.14836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many results in random matrix theory and high-dimensional statistics depend on weak convergence of spectral measures, which is usually established via pointwise convergence of Stieltjes transforms. This approach has recently been applied to signed measures. However, for signed measures, pointwise convergence of Stieltjes transforms alone no longer characterizes weak convergence. While this is unproblematic in many cases, in the high-dimensional regression setting, recently considered by Green and Romanov (2025), the underlying signed eigenvector-overlap measures can fail to converge weakly, despite pointwise convergence of their Stieltjes transforms. Using a novel approach to risk analysis, we show that weak convergence can be replaced by a simple convergence result for bilinear forms. This allows us to establish convergence of the prediction risk for estimators based on arbitrary continuous spectral filters, including (regularized) gradient descent and ridge regression, even when the underlying signed measures fail to converge weakly. Under additional regularity conditions, we construct an explicit finite signed measure yielding an integral representation of the asymptotic prediction risk. This representation provides necessary and sufficient conditions for minimum-norm interpolation and optimally tuned ridge regression to attain the smallest asymptotic prediction risk among estimators with continuous spectral filters. Moreover, we provide characterizations of weak and vague convergence of finite signed measures in terms of pointwise convergence of their Stieltjes transforms.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Stark, Georg K\"ostenberger, Nina D\"ornemann

item.title: Escaping the Curse of Dimensionality in One-Step Flow-Based Generative Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.15447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flow and diffusion-based generative models achieve state-of-the-art quality, but require multiple forward passes at inference time, making them computationally costly. Consistency models overcome this by learning a flow map directly, enabling few-step generation and dramatically reducing the computation needed at test time. However, formal statistical guarantees for such one-step generators are scarce. Existing results either suffer from the curse of dimensionality or rely on impractical loss functions. We investigate whether one-step flow-based models can escape the curse of dimensionality under the assumption that the data distribution is generated by a low-dimensional surface perturbed with Gaussian noise. In this setup, we derive approximation and generalization error bounds for the flow map estimate that circumvent the curse of dimensionality. Our findings provide the first principled explanation for practical success of one-step flow-based generative models.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Yakovlev

item.title: Statistical-to-computational gaps in central limit theorems for high-dimensional tensors
item.description: arXiv:2611.15803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study high-dimensional central limit theorems (CLTs) as hypothesis testing problems, comparing the number of summands needed for statistical and computational indistinguishability of the normalized sum from the limiting Gaussian distribution as the dimension and number of summands grow together. For the off-diagonal entries of sums of i.i.d. rank-one tensors formed from standard Gaussian vectors (equivalently, the problem of distinguishing Wigner from Wishart tensors), we prove total variation bounds sharpening previous estimates of Mikulincer (2020) and give matching polynomial-time tests. This shows that the statistical and computational thresholds coincide for this CLT, contrary to a proposal by Kunisky, Moore, and Wein (2024). On the other hand, we also show that, for tensors of order at least three, sufficient Gaussian dilution of the summands by adding independent Gaussian noise and rescaling gives a CLT model with a statistical-to-computational gap (in the above setting and ones with more general rank-one summand distributions). To the best of our knowledge, such a phenomenon has not been observed before in any high-dimensional CLT. In particular, in the relevant parameter regimes, we show that a brute-force search achieves strong detection, while polynomials of degree up to $n^{\Omega(1)}$ cannot achieve strong separation. The latter lower bounds control low-degree $\chi^2$-divergences by a novel method based on cumulant generating functions, and we further illustrate the use of these tools by applying them to masked tensor CLT models where only a prescribed subset of tensor entries is revealed.
item.dc:creator: Debsurya De, Dmitriy Kunisky

item.title: Beyond Curvature Bias: Higher-Order Manifold Fitting via Multiscale Cancellation
item.description: arXiv:2611.16235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local manifold-fitting procedures smooth noisy observations over neighborhoods of scale $h$, inducing a systematic normal bias of order $h^2+\sigma^2$ that persists at the population level. We develop geometric bias cancellation (GBC), a multiscale framework for higher-order manifold recovery under ambient Gaussian noise. For procedures admitting a normal-bias expansion $c(h,\sigma)b(x)+O(h^4)$, we construct cross-scale correspondence using estimated normal fibers and show that second-order normal accuracy suffices for fourth-order correspondence accuracy. Canceling the leading geometric bias yields $O(h^4)$ population Hausdorff accuracy while preserving an embedded manifold diffeomorphic to the underlying manifold. We establish the required expansions and finite-sample recovery guarantees for successive tangent-space projection and Gaussian density ridges. For STSP, geometric bias cancellation also achieves an asymptotically vanishing Hausdorff error ratio relative to oracle bandwidth-tuned single-scale fitting. For the local contraction estimator of \citet{yao2023manifold}, we identify an obstruction to scalar bias cancellation and develop a directional cancellation achieving $O(\sigma^4)$ population Hausdorff accuracy with uniform positive reach, as well as fourth-order finite-sample accuracy when $n\gtrsim\sigma^{-(d+6)}\log(1/\sigma)$. Simulations confirm the predicted improvement from second- to fourth-order population bias.
item.dc:creator: Zhijun Zhu, Haoyu Yang, Ruoyu Xiong, Bingjie Li, Zhigang Yao

item.title: Posterior contraction rates for banded approximations of Gaussian processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.16482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gaussian process regression models are widely used in modern statistics and machine learning due to their flexibility, interpretability, built-in uncertainty quantification, and strong theoretical foundations. However, training Gaussian processes (GPs) has a computational cost of $O(n^3)$, while the memory and prediction costs are also $O(n^2)$. For large datasets commonly encountered in practice, this becomes infeasible and necessitates the use of approximate posterior methods. In this work, we propose a class of approximations based on sparse covariance matrices, where the kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points. We analyze the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior distribution and show that the proposed approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties, provided that the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighboring points for each feature are retained. We derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbors required in a general setting and apply these results to standard kernels, including the squared exponential and Mat\'ern kernels. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Omar Kassi, Bernhard Stankewitz, Botond Szabo

item.title: Parameter estimation in models with explosive drift and Gaussian noise
item.description: arXiv:2611.16790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study drift parameter estimation for a positive stochastic process with singular mean-reverting drift driven by Gaussian noise. For Riemann-Liouville fractional Brownian noise with Hurst parameter $H>1/2$, an observable fractional transformation reduces the model to a semimartingale with drift linear in the unknown parameters. Using the quasi-likelihood approach, we derive explicit estimators of both drift coefficients. For a broader class of Gaussian driving processes, we construct a strongly consistent estimator of the ratio $a/b$, which has a natural mean-reversion interpretation, and verify the required assumptions for several Gaussian models. The theoretical results are complemented by a simulation study investigating the effects of the observation horizon and the discretization step on the finite-sample accuracy of the proposed estimators.
item.dc:creator: Yuliya Mishura, Kostiantyn Ralchenko, Mykyta Yakovliev

item.title: Automatic Threshold Selection Leaves Finite-Degree Bias in Network Power-Law Fits
item.description: arXiv:2611.16817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimum-distance fitting selects a degree threshold and a power-law exponent from the same network. We study the procedure that fits a continuous Pareto law with the Hill estimator and minimizes the Kolmogorov--Smirnov distance over retained ranks. For homogeneous linear preferential attachment and Norros--Reittu graphs with Pareto weights, we derive the joint limiting law of the selected rank, retained fraction of the threshold tie, and exponent error. The selector retains of order $n^{2/(\alpha+2)}$ of $n$ vertices, where $\alpha$ is the survival exponent. At this rank, integer spacing and finite-degree departures from a Pareto tail have the same order as sampling fluctuations. The exponent estimate is consistent and retains a shift on the scale used for confidence intervals. For integer degree laws whose tail sums have a first-order inverse-degree expansion, adding the retained tie fraction divided by the threshold to the Hill statistic removes the leading contribution of the tie. Under homogeneous preferential attachment with a fixed known number of edges per new vertex, removing the remaining model-specific term and calibrating for selection gives confidence intervals with asymptotically exact coverage. Observed networks show sensitivity of the fitted exponent and the classification of degree variance to threshold ties. Simulations assess interval coverage and show improved pooled connectivity predictions after correction under both specified graph laws. Changes to the Norros--Reittu weight distribution can reverse the prediction gain.
item.dc:creator: Tiandong Wang

item.title: Control Variates to reduce the variance of the empirical Moment Generating Function: an extreme value perspective
item.description: arXiv:2611.17016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate estimation of Moment Generating Functions is fundamental in many applications, but empirical estimators have high variances. Within a control variate setup, Extreme Value Theory is leveraged to identify how extreme values affect the variance reduction method's optimality.
item.dc:creator: Louison Bocquet-Nouaille, J\'er\^ome Morio, Benjamin Bobbia, Philippe Naveau

item.title: Isotonic least squares is robust to heteroscedasticity, unimodal least squares is not
item.description: arXiv:2611.17082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We compare the least squares estimator (LSE) with the $\ell_{1}$-estimator recently introduced by Baraud and Maillard~\citeyearpar{BM-2026} for estimating a regression function under a fixed design, when the errors are independent but possibly heteroscedastic and heavy-tailed. We show that the two estimators coincide on the class of nondecreasing (or nonincreasing) functions on an interval. As a consequence, the isotonic LSE inherits the non-asymptotic $\ell_{1}$-risk bounds of the $\ell_{1}$-estimator, which only require a moment of order $p\in[1,2]$ on the errors and depend on the average of their $p$-th absolute moments rather than on their maximum. This coincidence no longer holds on the nonconvex class of unimodal functions: we exhibit a heteroscedastic Gaussian example in which the LSE is inconsistent while the $\ell_{1}$-estimator converges at the parametric rate. Finally, we show on a one-dimensional linear model that neither estimator dominates the other: depending on the way the noise is distributed among the design points, the LSE may converge at rate $1/n$ while the $\ell_{1}$-estimator is inconsistent.
item.dc:creator: Yannick Baraud

item.title: Linear Regression with Self-Selection Bias in Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.17228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the problem of estimating $k$ linear regressors with self-selection bias in $n$ dimensions up to error $\varepsilon$ with the maximum self-selection criterion, as introduced by Cherapanamjeri, Daskalakis, Ilyas, and Zampetakis [CDIZ23, STOC]. Our main result is a $\mathrm{poly}(n,k,1/\varepsilon)$ time algorithm for the unknown-index variant of this problem, thereby improving upon the running times of the best known algorithms due to Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] and Kalavasis, Mehrotra, and Zhou [KMZ26, COLT] with exponential dependence on $k$. Our algorithm succeeds in the presence of correlated noise between regressors, which captures the related setting of max-affine regression. Consequently, we also give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, improving on the prior works of Ghosh, Pananjady, Guntuboyina, and Ramchandran [GPGR22, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory] and Gaitonde and Mossel [GM24] with exponential dependence on $k$. Prior works exhaustively search over a $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the regressors, using conditional moments of the response to test candidates. In contrast, our algorithm is driven by an improved understanding of the moments of the covariates. We show that, restricting to observations with large response values, the degree-$(\log n)$ Hermite moment of the covariates approximately decomposes as a sum of tensor powers of the regressors. The first step of our algorithm can be viewed as a tensor decomposition algorithm for these implicitly represented high-order tensors, which outputs unit vectors parallel to the regressors. A secondary step based on a simple variant of ordinary least squares extracts estimates for the regressors given these unit vectors. We believe our analytic insight and algorithmic components may have applications to designing efficient algorithms for other latent-variable problems.
item.dc:creator: Felix Zhou

item.title: The optimization landscape of robust high-dimensional mean estimation: stability, moment adaptation, and mirror descent reweighting
item.description: arXiv:2611.14966v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study efficient robust estimation of a high-dimensional mean under strong contamination when the clean distribution has only $p\ge2$ moments, bounded by $\nu_p$. We give a unified proof of stability for every $p\ge2$ with the optimal dimension-free sub-Gaussian rate, linking the reweighting, trimming and truncation techniques of the outlier and heavy-tailed robust literatures through concentration of counting and truncation processes. Building on stability and spectral signatures, we quantify the optimization landscape over sample weights that remove at most a fraction $\varepsilon_{n,k}=k/n$ of the mass, where the trimming parameter $k$ slightly exceeds the number of outliers. An unobserved convex spectral loss has inexact quadratic growth, with curvature $\frac{1-\varepsilon_{n,k}}{\varepsilon_{n,k}}$, relative to a mean-induced Bregman divergence, and the observable spectral loss supplies a dimension-free, inexact, relatively weakly star-convex subgradient oracle for it. This yields a Lyapunov analysis of mirror descent reweighting for $\varepsilon_{n,k}<\frac13$ that covers Hedge, the projected subgradient method, a new mean-induced mirror descent, and a centered multiplicative weights update. Each method uses one top-eigenvector computation per step and attains the optimal sub-Gaussian rate without knowledge of $(p,\nu_p)$. Mean-induced mirror descent further achieves faster optimization rates and last-iterate guarantees, at the cost of a more expensive projection step in higher dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Roberto I. Oliveira, Zoraida F. Rico, Philip Thompson

item.title: Moving Cut Loci and Gaussian Fluctuations of Intrinsic Huber Means on Compact Riemannian Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2611.15177v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Moving cut loci can change the limiting covariance of sample Huber means even when the cut locus of the population mean has probability zero. On a closed connected Riemannian manifold, we prove that the averaged logarithm field is $C^1$ near a point $m$ whenever the sampling law has a continuous density near its cut locus. The result holds for every continuous weight depending only on the observation, and the covariant derivative includes an explicit integral over the regular cut locus. When $m$ is a Huber mean for a fixed positive threshold, assume that the distance to $m$ has no atom at that threshold. The Hessian of the population risk then equals the expected pointwise Hessian minus a positive semidefinite cut locus correction. If $m$ is unique and this Hessian is positive definite, every measurable selection of global minimizers for i.i.d. samples satisfies a tangent-space central limit theorem. The cut loci of points in a ball of radius $\delta$ sweep out a region of volume $O(\delta)$, uniformly in the centre. These results establish the volume and integrability conditions previously assumed in a central limit theorem for intrinsic Fr\'echet means. At each fixed centre, the volume measure on this region, divided by $\delta$, converges weakly to an explicit measure on the regular cut locus. The Huber correction vanishes exactly when the region swept out about $m$ has probability $o(\delta)$.
item.dc:creator: Rui Qiu, Yiwei Yao, Zhou Yu

item.title: Can We Ignore Data Dependence in Inference Implementation? A Positive Answer for Regression Discontinuity Designs
item.description: arXiv:2611.15279v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In empirical economics, regression discontinuity design (RDD) inference is commonly based on asymptotic normality under an independence assumption, but the running variables or disturbances may exhibit unknown and complex dependence. We first rigorously identify a fundamental dilemma for this conventional practice. To address it, we propose a validity recovery procedure that redefines the roles of bias and stochastic calibration, thereby decoupling data dependence from stochastic calibration. Taking the independence-assumption-based confidence interval as our inferential anchor, our procedure restores its validity while preserving its asymptotic leading constant, even when the data are dependent. For fixed-design RDD based on local linear regression, our intervals achieve asymptotically exact nominal coverage and, compared with the anchor, exploit higher-order smoothness without enlarging the asymptotic variance constant, attaining the minimax-optimal shrinking rates up to a mild factor, such as $\sqrt{\log T})$. The procedure requires neither specific dependence frameworks (e.g., mixing or physical dependence) nor dependence-modeling techniques (e.g., long-run variance estimation). For random-design RDD, under more specific dependence assumptions, we derive the rate-explicit coverage error at each nominal level and characterize the trade-off between this rate and interval length. Moreover, modeling dependence becomes an optional enhancement that can further enable validity recovery and improve finite-sample coverage, while averaging over repeated calibrations stabilizes the randomized center and protects against undercoverage in finite samples without increasing interval length. In short, under mild dependence and moment conditions, our procedure makes data independence an implementation default rather than a validity requirement. Simulations support the theoretical results.
item.dc:creator: Zihao Yuan

item.title: Sharp Covering-Number Bounds for Feedforward ReLU Networks via Parameter Symmetries
item.description: arXiv:2611.15300v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In neural networks, distinct parameter configurations often realize the same input--output mapping, indicating that nominal parameter counts can overstate functional complexity. In this paper, we characterize the parameter-space symmetries of ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures. We prove that every quasianalytic parameter map preserving the network function is a composition of positive channel scaling and channel permutation. By quotienting out both symmetries, we derive uniform covering-number upper bounds in which positive scaling reduces the complexity exponent from the total parameter count $S$ to $S-H$ (with $H$ denoting the number of scalable channels) and permutation symmetry divides the bound by the factorial count $G$ of channel permutations. We establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponent $S-H$ is sharp in general and that the divisor $G$ is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks. We further extend these results to general continuous piecewise-linear activated networks. Finally, we apply our covering-number bounds to derive statistical risk guarantees for empirical risk minimization and capacity control beyond i.i.d.\ settings, and show how the underlying symmetries help explain weight rebalancing in function approximation and flat directions in empirical risk optimization.
item.dc:creator: Ruizhi Deng, Guohao Shen, Tangrui Xiong

item.title: VR-Net: Subarray-Level Inter-Cell Coordination for Multi-Cell XL-MIMO under Near-Field Spatial Non-Stationarity
item.description: arXiv:2611.15393v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial non-stationarity in multi-cell extremely large-scale MIMO (XL-MIMO) confines each user to a visibility region (VR) of each array. VR-Net exploits these regions for subarray-level coordinated beamforming. A base-station (BS)-indexed conflict graph identifies overlapping VRs; gain-based association and a masked multi-cell weighted minimum mean square error (WMMSE) iteration restrict beam design and channel state information (CSI) uploads to the relevant subarray blocks. We establish conditions for exact per-cell decoupling, derive the expected CSI loads, bound the loss of designing on the VR-gated channel and the loss of the support constraint, and characterize single-edge visibility contrast through a closed-form Fresnel transition width. Simulations use a 3GPP TR 38.901 Release-19-based near-field UMi channel with modular facade arrays and pre-registered criteria. At a 30 dB threshold, VR-Net retains at least 99.6% of the full-aperture WMMSE sum rate in every tested setting while uploading 10-39% fewer complex CSI entries. It gains up to 3.5 bit/s/Hz over an all-user adaptation of the multi-cell scheme of P\'erez-Ad\'an et al. at moderate power and dense load, and inter-cell coordination adds up to 33% over per-cell design.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Shoaib Ayub, Rana Muhammad Subhan, Insoo Koo, Felipe Augusto Pereira de Figueiredo

item.title: Sharp Gaussian approximation for Polyak--Ruppert averaged linear stochastic approximation
item.description: arXiv:2611.15442v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study how quickly the normalized Polyak--Ruppert average approaches its Gaussian limit in linear stochastic approximation with bounded i.i.d.\ coefficients. For step sizes decaying as $k^{-\gamma}$, with $1/2\le\gamma<1$, we prove an upper bound of order $n^{\gamma-1}$ on the approximation error over convex sets in fixed dimension. A matching lower bound holds for every fixed model. The fastest rate in this range is $n^{-1/2}$, attained at $\gamma=1/2$. We also obtain an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on the error of the recursive multiplier bootstrap procedure.
item.dc:creator: Bogdan Butyrin, Eric Moulines, Alexey Naumov, Sergey Samsonov

item.title: Controlling the Probability of Unknown Unknowns in Pre-Deployment Testing of AI Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.15835v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In pre-deployment testing of AI systems such as AI agents, a developer can often deal with known failure modes (e.g., leaking API keys, deleting important databases, or installing a malicious package) by implementing fixes or making contingency plans for when the same issue might occur again. What is more challenging are the unknown unknowns: the unseen failure modes that haven't surfaced during testing. The decision to stop testing and deploy therefore faces an inherent tradeoff: continue testing to observe more behaviors, at the cost of time and resources, or stop testing and deploy, at the risk of failure modes remaining undiscovered. How then does the developer decide when they have tested enough? To answer this, we develop an algorithm that certifies when the probability of observing an unseen failure mode is sufficiently small. The algorithm constructs an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence on this quantity, so the developer can repeatedly test a system, inspect the bound, and decide to stop when it falls below a chosen threshold without invalidating the statistical guarantee. Our problem can be interpreted as a sequential variant of the missing-mass estimation problem which gave rise to the classic Good-Turing estimator (Good, 1953). On SWE-Chat, a dataset of real-world coding agent traces (Baumann et al., 2026), we implement our procedure and show that it achieves tighter upper bounds than a simple multiple-testing corrected Good-Turing baseline, and even dominates a fixed-horizon (non-multiple-testing-corrected) Good-Turing upper confidence bound, which is not anytime valid. Additionally, to better match realistic evaluation pipelines, we extend our method to handle sampling from a different task distribution and imperfect automated failure labeling.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Li, Chris Hays, Aaditya Ramdas, Manish Raghavan

item.title: Zero detection via Cox random measures
item.description: arXiv:2611.16011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Using point process theory we propose and investigate a probabilistic identification of zeros of a deterministic real valued function. We construct a random atomic driving measure for a Cox point process whose mass at a candidate location depends explicitly on the value of the function at that location. We study the properties of the constructed random measure, including its exact asymptotic properties, its Laplace functional and related random processes. We also give an important application involving zero detection for Riemann's {\xi} function.
item.dc:creator: Athanasios Christou Micheas

item.title: Fr\'echet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.16209v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose Fr\'echet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fr\'echet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fr\'echet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.
item.dc:creator: Jiaye Chen, Rui Qiu, Zhou Yu

item.title: Sharp Bounds for Near-Maximizers of Gaussian Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.16233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a centered Gaussian process $G$ with continuous sample paths on a compact metric space $T$, a continuous drift $f: T \mapsto \mathbb{R}$, a noise level $\sigma>0$, and $\epsilon\ge 0$, let $A_\epsilon$ be the set of points at which $f+\sigma G$ is within $\epsilon$ of its maximum. Writing $\mathbb{E}\sup_TG$ for the expected supremum of $G$, we prove that the expected squared diameter of $A_\epsilon$ in the canonical pseudometric of $G$ is at most $8\epsilon \mathbb{E}\sup_TG/\sigma$ and that the expected maximal squared distance from a point of $A_\epsilon$ to an exact maximizer is at most $4\epsilon \mathbb{E}\sup_TG/\sigma$. The constants cannot be improved uniformly over index sets, processes, and drifts, and no logarithmic factor in $\epsilon$ appears, unlike in bounds integrated from tail estimates. At $\epsilon=0$ the bounds give the almost sure uniqueness of the maximizer in the canonical pseudometric without nondegeneracy assumptions. Given this uniqueness, both bounds follow from a bound with constant $2$ on the mean square of the largest increment of an independent copy of $G$ from an exact maximizer to a point of $A_\epsilon$. The proof rests on an identity for the mean squared support function of the $\epsilon$-subdifferentials of a smooth convex function at a standard Gaussian vector, obtained from two Gaussian integrations by parts.
item.dc:creator: Hirofumi Ota

item.title: On Ignorability Beyond Missing at Random: Completion-Invariant Missingness for Nonmonotone Missing Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.16278v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The missing-at-random assumption underlies most analyses of incomplete data. Under nonmonotone missingness, it is especially stringent, imposing pattern-specific restrictions with different conditioning sets. A strictly weaker normalization condition is known to justify maximizing the observed-data likelihood. We show that every law satisfying this condition has a unique missing-at-random counterpart sharing its observed-data and complete-data distributions. Observed-data procedures developed under missing at random for identified functionals, including doubly robust estimators, therefore remain valid, with the same semiparametric efficiency bound. We then prove that the condition holds if and only if filling in the missing values from their conditional distribution under the true full model preserves the complete-data distribution, hence the name completion-invariant missingness. We use a characteristic kernel to compare the completed distribution with the fitted model and assess the joint compatibility of the specified full model and completion-invariant missingness. We derive the asymptotic null distribution with estimated parameters and establish bootstrap and multiplier calibration. Since a parametric full model alone need not identify completion-invariant missingness, we give identification conditions for Gaussian, Student $t$ and finite mixture families. Simulations assess sensitivity to departures from each assumption, and applications to clinical laboratory measurements and childhood growth illustrate the diagnostic.
item.dc:creator: Kosuke Morikawa, Yutaka Kano, Shonosuke Sugasawa

item.title: Optimal Sample Complexity for Genus-Two Zeta Functions from Noisy Random Euler Products
item.description: arXiv:2611.16358v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study exact recovery of the Hasse--Weil zeta numerator from repeated noisy observations of a randomized Euler product. For a genus-two curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$, we attach independent symmetric signs to its closed points and observe the logarithm of the resulting product at $t_q=c/\sqrt q$, where $0<c<1/\sqrt{12}$ is fixed. For every fixed, known additive noise density $f$ satisfying $\sqrt{f}\in H^1(\mathbb{R})$, we prove that the minimax number of independent observations required for exact recovery with error probability at most $\delta$ has order $q^4\log(1/\delta)$. No moment condition is imposed on the noise, so the result includes Cauchy readout. The upper bound estimates the phase of an empirical characteristic function and uses the separation of the integral Weil coefficients. The matching lower bound compares the full observation laws for two actual curves with ordinary, absolutely simple Jacobians. It combines a binomial comparison with a uniform bound on the closed-point tail. Thus access to the full observations does not improve the sample order attained by the phase estimator. The result concerns the information in a specified observation channel. It does not assume an efficient implementation of that channel.
item.dc:creator: Taro Hayashi, Ryoichi Suzuki

item.title: Nonsense nonlinear correlations between independent random walks
item.description: arXiv:2611.16614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sample distance correlation can remain large between independent random walks. For centred walks with independent, identically distributed increments of finite, positive variance, we prove convergence in distribution to the distance correlation of the joint occupation measure of two independent Brownian paths. This universal limit lies strictly between zero and one almost surely and has full support on the unit interval. We calculate the expected squared distance covariance of the limiting measure and show that ordinary permutation calibration rejects independence with probability tending to one at every fixed nominal level. Gaussian simulations illustrate the persistent dispersion of random-walk correlations and the failure of permutation calibration.
item.dc:creator: Liping Zhu, Zhongming Xie

item.title: Unequal-probability distributional balance and the Horvitz-Thompson estimator
item.description: arXiv:2611.17273v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Auxiliary information can improve estimation precision under probability sampling, but the relationship between the study and auxiliary variables may not be known well enough to specify suitable balancing variables. Distributionally balanced designs address this by targeting agreement between sample and population auxiliary distributions. We extend energy-based distributional balance to prescribed unequal inclusion probabilities by comparing the empirical sample distribution with an inclusion-probability-weighted population distribution. Under a regularity condition relating the study values divided by their inclusion probabilities to the auxiliaries, we establish an upper bound on the design variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator in terms of the expected energy distance. This bound motivates an algorithm that exchanges units between randomly paired candidate samples without increasing their average energy distance. Combined with random initialization and uniform selection of a final candidate, the procedure preserves the prescribed first-order inclusion probabilities. We evaluate its auxiliary-space properties and estimation performance using generated populations and the Meuse data.
item.dc:creator: Blair Robertson, Chris Price, Marco Reale, Philip Davies

item.title: Testing the number of common factors by bootstrapped sample covariance matrix in high-dimensional factor models and errata
item.description: arXiv:2202.06188v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the impact of bootstrap procedure on the eigenvalue distributions of the sample covariance matrix under a high-dimensional factor structure. We provide asymptotic distributions for the top eigenvalues of bootstrapped sample covariance matrix under mild conditions. After bootstrap, the spiked eigenvalues which are driven by common factors will converge weakly to Gaussian limits after proper scaling and centralization. However, the largest non-spiked eigenvalue is mainly determined by the order statistics of the bootstrap resampling weights, and follows extreme value distribution. Based on the disparate behavior of the spiked and non-spiked eigenvalues, we propose innovative methods to test the number of common factors. Indicated by extensive numerical and empirical studies, the proposed methods perform reliably and convincingly under the existence of both weak factors and cross-sectionally correlated errors. Our technical details contribute to random matrix theory on spiked covariance model with convexly decaying density and unbounded support, or with general elliptical distributions.
item.dc:creator: Long Yu, Peng Zhao, Wang Zhou

item.title: A sharper bound of the Hotelling-Solomons inequality
item.description: arXiv:2310.10303v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The original Hotelling-Solomons inequality states that an upper bound of the absolute difference between the mean and median, standardized by the standard deviation, is 1. However, in this paper, we introduce a new bound that depends on the sample size, which is strictly smaller than 1.
item.dc:creator: Yuzo Maruyama

item.title: Drift Parameter Estimation for an Ergodic Extension of the Double Heston Model
item.description: arXiv:2501.17100v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The double Heston model is a widely used stochastic volatility model in financial mathematics, particularly for option pricing, risk management, and volatility surface calibration. This paper investigates the joint estimation of the drift parameters for an ergodic extension of the double Heston model. We first establish stochastic properties of the underlying process, including the existence of a stationary distribution and ergodicity. We then study maximum likelihood and conditional least squares estimators based on continuous-time observations. For both estimation procedures, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality under suitable ergodicity conditions.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Ben Alaya, Houssem Dahbi, Hamdi Fathallah

item.title: Beyond Brown's radial tests: admissibility, parabolicity, and a doubling-Poincar\'e prior that neither test decides
item.description: arXiv:2610.34309v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For the estimation of a normal mean in $\mathbb{R}^m$ under quadratic loss, Brown (1971) proved that a generalized Bayes estimator $\delta_F$ with bounded drift is admissible if and only if a diffusion attached to the marginal $f^*$ of the prior $F$ is recurrent, and gave two radial tests: a sphere-average test for recurrence and a ray test for transience. He observed that both tests can be silent. We read his theory as the potential theory of the weighted Euclidean space $(\mathbb{R}^m,f^*\,dx)$ and ask what the modern theory of recurrence on weighted manifolds adds inside the zone where neither test applies. Three results. (A) If $f^*\,dx$ is doubling and supports a scale-invariant Poincar\'e inequality, the sphere test is already complete: recurrence, Brown's sphere test and the ball-volume test are equivalent, so geometric criteria can add decidable cases only on the inadmissible side. (B) They do add one. An explicit prior on $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose marginal is small along a lattice of circles at dyadic scales with spacing equal to the square root of the scale is doubling and Poincar\'e, silences both of Brown's tests, and is transient by the ball-volume test; its generalized Bayes estimator is inadmissible. (C) Outside the doubling-Poincar\'e class the zone is two-sided: similar circles placed on one surface per scale give an admissible estimator, decided by a flux bound along a non-spherical exhaustion, and a logarithmic product prior gives an inadmissible one, decided by product heat kernels. A comparison lemma shows that any positive weight with Lipschitz logarithm is, up to constants, the marginal of a prior, so that explicit weights may be used throughout.
item.dc:creator: Oleg Roshka

item.title: A Spectral Boundary for Independence Learnability
item.description: arXiv:2610.38999v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learning independence is fundamental to statistical inference and machine learning, yet learning independence between entire time series by a test remains challenging when only a single observation record is available. Existing guarantees often rely on structural or mixing assumptions, while stationarity and ergodicity alone do not permit consistent testing. In this work, we identify a class-level boundary governed by shared nontrivial Koopman eigenvalues, which represent common persistent oscillatory frequencies of the two processes. When no such eigenvalues are shared, we extend shift-based rank calibration with finite-window dependence witnesses and a data-adaptive threshold to construct a deterministic, weakly consistent test with finite-sample false-positive control, without quantitative mixing assumptions. Conversely, we show that no possibly randomized test can achieve vanishing false-positive probabilities under every independent jointly totally ergodic law while consistently detecting every dependent jointly totally ergodic law with a shared nontrivial eigenvalue. This impossibility already holds when the shared point spectrum is exactly the cyclic group generated by any single prescribed irrational eigenfrequency, identifying a spectral obstruction to universal learning of full-process independence.
item.dc:creator: Senhan Yao, Yuxin Zhou

item.title: Local Fr\'echet regression with polyspherical predictors: Uniform convergence rates and factor selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.13240v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study local Fr\'echet regression for responses taking values in a metric space and predictors on a product of spheres of possibly different dimensions. We propose local constant and local linear estimators with factor-specific bandwidths and establish uniform convergence rates. We select sphere factors by comparing cross-fitted prediction risks for the full and leave-one-factor-out models. The procedure consistently recovers the active factor set, and the selected local constant and local linear estimators attain the same uniform convergence rates as if the active factor set were known. For univariate Wasserstein responses supported on a common compact interval, the uniform rate holds without an entropy condition on the response space. Simulations with scalar and spherical responses and analyses of vessel speeds and drifter speed distributions illustrate the methods.
item.dc:creator: Chang Jun Im

item.title: On the modelling and prediction of high-dimensional functional time series
item.description: arXiv:2406.00700v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a two-step procedure to model and predict high-dimensional functional time series, where the number of function-valued time series $p$ is large in relation to the length of time series $n$. Our first step performs an eigenanalysis of a positive definite matrix, which leads to a one-to-one linear transformation for the original high-dimensional functional time series, and the transformed curve series can be segmented into several groups such that any two subseries from any two different groups are uncorrelated both contemporaneously and serially. Consequently in our second step those groups are handled separately without the information loss on the overall linear dynamic structure. The second step is devoted to establishing a finite-dimensional dynamical structure for all the transformed functional time series within each group. Furthermore the finite-dimensional structure is represented by that of a vector time series. Modelling and forecasting for the original high-dimensional functional time series are realized via those for the vector time series in all the groups. We investigate the theoretical properties of our proposed methods, and illustrate the finite-sample performance through both extensive simulation and two real datasets.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Qin Fang, Xinghao Qiao, Qiwei Yao

item.title: Optimal linear filtering of partially observed polynomial processes in discrete and continuous time
item.description: arXiv:2503.05588v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper is devoted to filtering, smoothing, and prediction of polynomial processes that are partially observed. These problems are known to allow for an explicit solution in the simpler case of linear Gaussian state space models. The key insight underlying the present piece of research is that in linear filtering applications polynomial processes and their discrete-time counterpart are indistinguishable from Gaussian processes sharing their first two moments. We describe the construction of these Gaussian equivalents of polynomial processes and explicitly compute optimal linear filters, predictors and smoothers for polynomial processes in discrete and continuous time. The consideration of Gaussian equivalents also opens the door to parameter estimation and linear-quadratic optimal control in the context of polynomial processes.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kallsen, Ivo Richert

item.title: PAC Reasoning: Controlling the Performance Loss for Efficient Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2510.09133v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable progress in complex problem-solving tasks. Despite this success, LRMs typically suffer from high computational costs during deployment, highlighting a need for efficient inference. A practical direction is to switch the LRM between thinking and non-thinking modes dynamically. However, such approaches often introduce additional reasoning errors and lack statistical guarantees for the performance loss, which are critical for high-stakes applications. In this work, we propose Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Reasoning that controls the performance loss under the user-specified tolerance. Specifically, we construct an upper confidence bound on the performance loss and determine a threshold for switching to the non-thinking model. Theoretically, using the threshold to switch between the thinking and non-thinking modes ensures bounded performance loss in a distribution-free manner. Our experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed method can save computational budgets and control the user-specified performance loss.
item.dc:creator: Hao Zeng, Jianguo Huang, Bingyi Jing, Hongxin Wei, Bo An

item.title: Universal concentration for sums under arbitrary dependence
item.description: arXiv:2601.03518v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a universal concentration bound for sums of random variables under arbitrary dependence, and we prove that it is asymptotically optimal for broad families of marginals admitting a uniform integrable tail-quantile envelope. The bound follows directly from the subadditivity of expected shortfall, a property well known in the risk-measure literature. Our sharpness result relies on an explicit construction of asymptotically extremal couplings. We furthermore provide practical sufficient conditions -- based on convex transformation order comparisons with exponential and power-law envelopes -- under which the bound admits simple, explicit tail profiles.
item.dc:creator: Cosme Louart, Sicheng Tan

item.title: Functional Stochastic Localization
item.description: arXiv:2602.03999v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Eldan's stochastic localization is a probabilistic construction that has proved instrumental to modern breakthroughs in high-dimensional geometry and the design of sampling algorithms. Motivated by sampling under non-Euclidean geometries and the mirror descent algorithm in optimization, we develop a functional generalization of Eldan's process that replaces Gaussian regularization with regularization by any positive integer multiple of a log-Laplace transform. We further give a mixing time bound on the Markov chain induced by our localization process, which holds if our target distribution satisfies a functional Poincar\'e inequality. Finally, we apply our framework to differentially private convex optimization in $\ell_p$ norms for $p \in [1, 2)$, where we improve state-of-the-art query complexities in a zeroth-order model.
item.dc:creator: Anming Gu, Bobby Shi, Kevin Tian

item.title: Sequential Membership Inference Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2602.16596v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern AI models are not static. They go through multiple updates in their lifecycles. We propose to design Sequential Membership Inference (SeMI) attacks leading to tighter privacy audits by exploiting the sequence of models and injecting a target canary at a controlled insertion time. First, for empirical mean computation, we develop SeMI*, an optimal SeMI attack to identify the presence of a target inserted at a specific insertion step. We derive the power of SeMI* to show that accessing the model sequence yields more powerful MI attacks than scrutinising only the final model. SeMI* exhibits an isolation property. Its power depends on the statistics obtained right before and after insertion of the target. Leveraging this insight, we develop practical white-box (accessing model gradients) and black-box (accessing loss) SeMI attacks against models trained with (DP-)SGD. Across datasets and models trained with (DP-)SGD, our experiments show that SeMI attacks achieve higher power than snapshot-independent baselines, and yield tighter privacy audits thanks to (a) control over the insertion time and (b) observations across the model sequence. Code is available at https://github.com/Thomick/pysemi.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Michel, Debabrota Basu, Emilie Kaufmann

item.title: On the Uniqueness of Fr\'echet Means for Polytope Norms
item.description: arXiv:2603.15785v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fr\'echet means are a popular type of average for non-Euclidean datasets, defined as those points that minimise the average squared distance to a set of data points. We consider the behaviour of sample Fr\'echet means on normed spaces whose unit ball is a polytope; this setting is particularly important for semi-discrete data, but is rarely covered by existing literature on Fr\'echet means, which focuses primarily on manifolds and spaces with bounded Alexandrov curvature. We study the geometry of the set of Fr\'echet means over polytope normed spaces, with a focus on dimension and probabilistic conditions for uniqueness. In particular, we provide a geometric characterisation of the threshold sample size at which Fr\'echet means have a positive probability of being unique, and we prove that this threshold is at most one more than the dimension of our space. This geometric characterisation presents a novel framework for computing the unique Fr\'echet mean sample threshold, which we demonstrate in the case of the $\ell_1$, $\ell_{\infty}$ and tropical norms. In particular, we show that the $\ell_1$ sample threshold is always 3, but the $\ell_{\infty}$ and tropical sample thresholds grow at different rates with the dimension of our space.
item.dc:creator: Roan Talbut, Andrew McCormack, Anthea Monod

item.title: Pseudo-Labeling for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation with Kernel GLMs
item.description: arXiv:2603.19422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a principled framework for unsupervised domain adaptation under covariate shift in kernel Generalized Linear Models (GLMs), encompassing kernelized linear, logistic, and Poisson regression with ridge regularization. Our goal is to minimize prediction error in the target domain by leveraging labeled source data and unlabeled target data, despite differences in covariate distributions. We partition the labeled source data into two batches: one for training a family of candidate models, and the other for building an imputation model. This imputation model generates pseudo-labels for the target data, enabling robust model selection. We establish non-asymptotic excess-risk bounds that characterize adaptation performance through an "effective labeled sample size", explicitly accounting for the unknown covariate shift. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate consistent performance gains over source-only baselines.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Weill, Kaizheng Wang

item.title: Maximum score and non-smooth M-estimators with multiway dependence
item.description: arXiv:2604.10232v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Under i.i.d. sampling, the maximum score estimator of Manski (1975) converges at the cube-root rate to a non-Gaussian limit, and under median independence alone no regular estimator attains the parametric rate Chamberlain (1986). We show that, under multiway dependence and low-level conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal at a parametric rate in the smallest number of clusters and, when the cluster-level variance is non-degenerate, as fast as regular estimators such as probit. The result rests on a general theory for non-smooth M-estimators, under which a modified bootstrap is first-order valid given a consistent Hessian estimate. With two-way clustering a cube-root term can remain. We then develop two-scale non-standard asymptotics, in which the limit is a Gaussian vector plus an independent Chernoff-type vector and either term may dominate, along sequences of laws from a non-degenerate cluster-level variance to the degenerate case. Under high-level conditions, the symmetric bootstrap intervals for suitable scalar parameters control size uniformly over such classes of laws, asymptotically exactly where the Gaussian term dominates and conservatively otherwise.
item.dc:creator: Harold D. Chiang, Ahnaf Rafi

item.title: Cloning is as Hard as Learning for Stabilizer States
item.description: arXiv:2604.15269v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The impossibility of simultaneously cloning non-orthogonal states lies at the foundations of quantum theory. Even when allowing for approximation errors, cloning an arbitrary unknown pure state requires as many initial copies as needed to fully learn the state. Rather than arbitrary unknown states, modern quantum learning theory often considers structured classes of states and exploits such structure to develop learning algorithms that outperform general-state tomography. This raises the question: How do the sample complexities of learning and cloning relate for such structured classes. We answer this question for an important class of states. Namely, for $n$-qubit stabilizer states, we show that the optimal sample complexity of cloning is $\Theta(n)$. Thus, also for this structured class of states, cloning is as hard as learning. To prove this result, we relate stabilizer state cloning to a variant of the sample amplification problem for probability distributions that was recently introduced in classical learning theory. This allows us to obtain our cloning lower bounds in analogy to new sample amplification lower bounds for classes of distributions with an underlying linear structure. Our results provide a more fine-grained perspective on No-Cloning theorems, opening up connections from foundations to quantum learning theory and quantum cryptography.
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Bansal, Matthias C. Caro, Gaurav Mahajan

item.title: Small area learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.15953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a novel learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop estimators with and without cross-fitting, accommodating low-complexity and flexible learners and unifying synthetic, model-based, and semi-supervised estimators. For area means, we establish a unified asymptotic theory for these estimator families, characterizing conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality and providing variance estimators and confidence intervals without prescribing a particular learning algorithm. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals clearly a bias-variance trade-off: partial residual correction in classical estimators can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to the misspecification of working models, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34%-49% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Katarzyna Reluga, Nicola Salvati, Setareh Ranjbar, Nikos Tzavidis, Mark van der Laan

item.title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.14457v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised. We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to na\"ive KM risks. The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.
item.dc:creator: Ferran Espuny-Pujol
